questionText: Find the area of a rectangle with length 15 cm and width 11 cm.
hints: This is an area problem. Area is the space inside a shape, counted in squares.
Picture the rectangle filled with squares of 1 cm: 15 squares along the length, in 11 rows. Think about which operation counts them all.
Similar example: a rectangle 7 cm long and 4 cm wide holds 4 rows of 7 squares, so its area is 7 × 4 = 28 sq. cm.

stepByStep.text: The area of a rectangle is its length times its width. Here the length is 15 cm and the width is 11 cm.
Multiply 15 by 11 in two parts: 15 × 10 = 150 and 15 × 1 = 15. Add them: 150 + 15 = 165.
So the area of the rectangle is 165 sq. cm.

misconceptions.A: 26 is 15 + 11. Area counts the squares that fill the rectangle, so think of rows of squares.
misconceptions.B: 330 is 2 × 15 × 11. The doubling belongs to perimeter. For area, multiply the length and width only.
misconceptions.C: 52 is the distance around the rectangle, 15 + 11 + 15 + 11. The question asks for the space inside it.
misconceptions.D: That's it! 11 rows of 15 squares fill the rectangle, and 15 × 11 = 165 sq. cm.

questionText: Find the area of a rectangle with length 24 cm and width 11 cm.
hints: This is an area problem. Area is the space inside a shape, counted in squares.
Picture the rectangle filled with squares of 1 cm: 24 squares along the length, in 11 rows. Think about which operation counts them all.
Similar example: a rectangle 14 cm long and 6 cm wide holds 6 rows of 14 squares, so its area is 14 × 6 = 84 sq. cm.

stepByStep.text: The area of a rectangle is its length times its width. Here the length is 24 cm and the width is 11 cm.
Multiply 24 by 11 in two parts: 24 × 10 = 240 and 24 × 1 = 24. Add them: 240 + 24 = 264.
So the area of the rectangle is 264 sq. cm.

misconceptions.A: 70 is 2 × (24 + 11), which is the perimeter, the distance around. Area is the space inside.
misconceptions.B: 528 is 2 × 24 × 11. The doubling belongs to perimeter. For area, multiply the length and width only.
misconceptions.C: That's it! 11 rows of 24 squares fill the rectangle, and 24 × 11 = 264 sq. cm.
misconceptions.D: 35 is 24 + 11. Area counts the squares that fill the rectangle, so think of rows of squares.

questionText: Find the perimeter of a rectangle with length 25 cm and width 3 cm.
hints: The question asks for perimeter. Imagine walking along every side of the rectangle until you are back where you started.
A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. Here that means two sides of 25 cm and two sides of 3 cm, and all four are counted.
Similar example: a rectangle 20 cm long and 7 cm wide has sides of 20, 7, 20 and 7 cm. Its perimeter is 20 + 7 + 20 + 7 = 54 cm.

stepByStep.text: Perimeter is the distance around the rectangle, so all four sides are added: two lengths of 25 cm and two widths of 3 cm.
One length and one width together make 25 + 3 = 28 cm.
There are two of each, so double it: 2 × 28 = 56. The perimeter is 56 cm.

misconceptions.A: 75 is 25 × 3, which is the area. Perimeter is the distance around, so the sides are added.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Perimeter is all four sides added: 25 + 3 + 25 + 3 = 56 cm.
misconceptions.C: 53 is 25 + 25 + 3. One side is still missing, because a rectangle has four sides.
misconceptions.D: 28 is 25 + 3, which is only halfway around the rectangle. Keep going along the other two sides.

questionText: Find the perimeter of a rectangle with length 15 cm and width 9 cm.
hints: This is a perimeter problem. Perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape.
A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. Here that means two sides of 15 cm and two sides of 9 cm, and all four are counted.
Similar example: a rectangle 10 cm long and 3 cm wide has sides of 10, 3, 10 and 3 cm. Its perimeter is 10 + 3 + 10 + 3 = 26 cm.

stepByStep.text: Perimeter is the distance around the rectangle, so all four sides are added: two lengths of 15 cm and two widths of 9 cm.
One length and one width together make 15 + 9 = 24 cm.
There are two of each, so double it: 2 × 24 = 48. The perimeter is 48 cm.

misconceptions.A: 24 is 15 + 9, just one length and one width. Walk all the way around: there are four sides.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Perimeter is all four sides added: 15 + 9 + 15 + 9 = 48 cm.
misconceptions.C: 39 is 15 + 15 + 9. One side is still missing, because a rectangle has four sides.
misconceptions.D: 135 is 15 × 9, which is the area. Perimeter is the distance around, so the sides are added.

questionText: Find the area of a rectangle with length 16 cm and width 4 cm.
hints: This is an area problem. Area is the space inside a shape, counted in squares.
Imagine 4 rows of small squares with 16 squares in each row. How would you count all the squares without counting one by one?
Similar example: a rectangle 6 cm long and 5 cm wide holds 5 rows of 6 squares, so its area is 6 × 5 = 30 sq. cm.

stepByStep.text: The area of a rectangle is its length times its width. Here the length is 16 cm and the width is 4 cm.
Multiply: 16 × 4 = 64.
So the area of the rectangle is 64 sq. cm.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Area is length times width, and 16 × 4 = 64 sq. cm.
misconceptions.B: 40 is the distance around the rectangle, 16 + 4 + 16 + 4. The question asks for the space inside it.
misconceptions.C: 128 is 16 × 4 and then doubled. Area is length times width just once.
misconceptions.D: 20 is 16 + 4. Area counts the squares that fill the rectangle, so think of rows of squares.

questionText: Rectangle length 2 more than width. Length=8ft. Area?
hints: To find the area of a rectangle you need both its length and its width. One of them is hidden inside a clue.
The length is 8 ft, and it is 2 more than the width. Work out the width first.
Here is a similar one: the length is 3 more than the width, and the length is 10 m. Width = 10 − 3 = 7 m. Area = 10 × 7 = 70 square metres.

stepByStep.text: The length is 2 more than the width, so the width is 2 less than the length.
Area is length × width.
So the area is 48 square feet.

misconceptions.A: This is 8 × 2. The 2 only tells you how much shorter the width is. The width is 8 − 2.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The width is 6 ft, and 8 × 6 = 48.
misconceptions.C: Check the width first: 8 − 2 = 6. Then multiply 8 × 6.
misconceptions.D: This is double the area. The width is 6 ft, so multiply 8 × 6 just once.

questionText: Wire bent into rectangle 16×12cm. Same wire bent into square. Side?
hints: The same wire makes both shapes, so the distance round each shape is the same.
Find the length of the wire first. It is the perimeter of the rectangle: two lengths and two widths.
Here is a similar one: a wire makes a rectangle 10 cm by 6 cm. Wire length = 2 × (10 + 6) = 32 cm. Bent into a square, each side is 32 ÷ 4 = 8 cm.

stepByStep.text: Add the length and the width of the rectangle.
Double it to get the whole wire.
The square uses the same 56 cm of wire for 4 equal sides.
So the side of the square is 14 cm.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The wire is 56 cm long, and 56 ÷ 4 = 14.
misconceptions.B: This is 16 + 12, only half of the wire. Double it, then share it among the 4 sides.
misconceptions.C: Check the wire length: 2 × (16 + 12) = 56 cm. Then divide by 4.
misconceptions.D: This is 28 ÷ 4. The whole wire is 56 cm, not 28 cm.

questionText: Perimeter of square a = 28cm. Area of rectangle 3a × 2a?
hints: First find the side of the square. Then use it to build the rectangle.
A square has 4 equal sides. Divide the perimeter, 28 cm, by 4 to find a.
Here is a similar one: a square of side a has perimeter 20 cm, so a = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm. A rectangle 3a by 2a is 15 cm by 10 cm. Area = 15 × 10 = 150 cm².

stepByStep.text: A square has 4 equal sides. Find the side a.
The rectangle is 3a long and 2a wide. That is 3 × 7 = 21 cm and 2 × 7 = 14 cm.
Multiply to find the area. Use 21 × 10 = 210 and 21 × 4 = 84.
The area is 294 cm², which is not among the numbers given. So the answer is None.

misconceptions.A: Work out the sides first: 3a = 21 cm and 2a = 14 cm. Then find 21 × 14.
misconceptions.B: This is close, but check 21 × 14 again. 210 + 84 does not make this number.
misconceptions.C: 245 is 5 × 7 × 7. The rectangle is 3a by 2a, so it holds 6 squares of 7 × 7.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The area is 21 × 14 = 294 cm², and that number is not listed.

questionText: Perimeter of square = 132cm. Area?
hints: You are given the distance round a square and asked for the space inside it. Find the side first.
A square has 4 equal sides. Divide the perimeter, 132 cm, by 4.
Here is a similar one: a square has perimeter 48 cm. Side = 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm. Area = 12 × 12 = 144 square cm.

stepByStep.text: A square has 4 equal sides. Find one side.
Area is side × side. Start with 33 × 30.
Then 33 × 3.
Add the two parts.
The side is in cm, so the area is in square cm. So the area is 1089 cm.sq.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The side is 33 cm, and 33 × 33 = 1089 square cm.
misconceptions.B: Two digits have swapped places here, and the unit should be square cm. 33 × 33 = 1089.
misconceptions.C: 961 is 31 × 31. The side is 132 ÷ 4 = 33 cm. Check the unit as well.
misconceptions.D: The number is right, but look at the unit. The sides are in cm, so the area is in square cm, not square m.

questionText: Perimeter of square and equilateral triangle are same. Side of triangle=12cm. Area of square?
hints: Both shapes have the same distance round them. Use the triangle to find that distance, then use it for the square.
An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides. Find its perimeter from the side of 12 cm.
Here is a similar one: the triangle's side is 20 cm. Perimeter = 3 × 20 = 60 cm. The square's side = 60 ÷ 4 = 15 cm. Area = 15 × 15 = 225 sq.cm.

stepByStep.text: The triangle has 3 equal sides of 12 cm. Find its perimeter.
The square has the same perimeter, shared among 4 equal sides.
Area of the square is side × side.
So the area of the square is 81 sq.cm.

misconceptions.A: 64 is 8 × 8. Check the square's side: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm.
misconceptions.B: 100 is 10 × 10. Check the square's side: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The perimeter is 36 cm, the square's side is 9 cm, and 9 × 9 = 81.
misconceptions.D: This is 12 × 12, but 12 cm is the triangle's side. The square's side is 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm.

questionText: The perimeter of a square is equal to the perimeter of an equilateral triangle. Each side of the triangle is 16 cm. What is the area of the square?
hints: Use the triangle to find the perimeter the two shapes share. Then use that perimeter to find the side of the square, and last its area.
An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides, so find its perimeter: 3 × 16 cm. The square has the same perimeter, shared equally among 4 sides.
Similar example: an equilateral triangle of side 8 cm has perimeter 3 × 8 = 24 cm. A square with the same perimeter has side 24 ÷ 4 = 6 cm, and its area is 6 × 6 = 36 sq cm.

stepByStep.text: Perimeter of the triangle: 3 equal sides of 16 cm.
The square has the same perimeter, 48 cm, shared among 4 equal sides.
Area of the square is side times side. The area is 144 cm.sq.

misconceptions.A: 256 is 16 × 16, which treats 16 cm as the side of the square. 16 cm is the side of the triangle, so find the perimeter first.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The perimeter is 3 × 16 = 48 cm, the side of the square is 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm, and 12 × 12 = 144.
misconceptions.C: This needs a square of side 10 cm, with perimeter 40 cm. The shared perimeter is 3 × 16 = 48 cm.
misconceptions.D: Check the side of the square: 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm. The area is side times side, 12 × 12.

questionText: Eight equal circles are drawn inside a rectangle in 2 rows of 4. Each circle just touches the circles next to it and the nearest sides of the rectangle. The radius of each circle is 4 cm. What is the area of the rectangle?
hints: The circles fill the rectangle exactly, so its length and breadth can be counted in circle widths. The width of a circle is its diameter.
Find the diameter of one circle: it is twice the radius of 4 cm. The length of the rectangle is 4 diameters and the breadth is 2 diameters.

Similar example: 6 equal circles of radius 5 cm sit in a rectangle in 2 rows of 3. The diameter is 10 cm. The length is 3 × 10 = 30 cm and the breadth is 2 × 10 = 20 cm, so the area is 30 × 20 = 600 sq cm.

stepByStep.text: The diameter of each circle is twice the radius.
The length holds 4 circles side by side.
The breadth holds 2 circles.
Area is length times breadth. The area of the rectangle is 512 cm.sq.

misconceptions.A: 256 is 16 × 16, which uses 16 cm for the length as well as the breadth. The length holds 4 whole circles: 4 × 8 = 32 cm.
misconceptions.B: Check the sides again. The length is 4 diameters, 32 cm, and the breadth is 2 diameters, 16 cm. Multiply those two.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The diameter is 8 cm, so the rectangle is 32 cm by 16 cm, and 32 × 16 = 512.
misconceptions.D: This is a little too big. The rectangle is exactly 4 diameters long and 2 diameters wide: 32 cm by 16 cm.

questionText: Perimeter of rectangle = 76cm. Which CANNOT be length and breadth?
hints: The perimeter is two lengths and two breadths. So one length and one breadth together make half of the perimeter.
Find half of 76. Then add each pair and see which pair does not make that number.
Here is a similar one: the perimeter is 40 cm, so length and breadth add up to 20 cm. 12 cm and 8 cm can be the sides, because 12 + 8 = 20. 14 cm and 7 cm cannot, because 14 + 7 = 21.

stepByStep.text: Length and breadth together make half of the perimeter.
Check the pairs: 22 + 16 = 38, 11 + 27 = 38 and 29 + 9 = 38. These three all fit.
Now check the last pair.
40 is not 38. So 24cm & 16cm cannot be the length and breadth.

misconceptions.A: 22 + 16 = 38, and that is half of 76. So this pair can be the sides. Look for the pair that does not add up to 38.
misconceptions.B: 11 + 27 = 38, and that is half of 76. So this pair can be the sides. Look for the pair that does not add up to 38.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 24 + 16 = 40, which would give a perimeter of 80 cm, not 76 cm.
misconceptions.D: 29 + 9 = 38, and that is half of 76. So this pair can be the sides. Look for the pair that does not add up to 38.

questionText: Breadth of rectangle = 12cm, perimeter = 52cm. Area?
hints: To find the area you need the length as well as the breadth. The perimeter helps you find the length.
Length and breadth together make half of the perimeter. Find half of 52 first.
Here is a similar one: the breadth is 5 cm and the perimeter is 30 cm. Half of 30 is 15, so the length is 15 − 5 = 10 cm. Area = 10 × 5 = 50 cm sq.

stepByStep.text: Length and breadth together make half of the perimeter.
Take away the breadth to get the length.
Area is length × breadth. Use 14 × 10 = 140 and 14 × 2 = 28.
So the area is 168 cm sq.

misconceptions.A: 156 is 13 × 12. Check the length: 26 − 12 = 14 cm.
misconceptions.B: 192 is 16 × 12. Check the length: 26 − 12 = 14 cm.
misconceptions.C: Check 14 × 12 once more: 14 × 10 = 140 and 14 × 2 = 28. Add those two.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The length is 14 cm, and 14 × 12 = 168.

questionText: A rectangle has:
hints: Think about the corners of a rectangle, like the corners of your notebook.
A right angle is a square corner. Count the corners of a rectangle and check each one.
Here is a similar idea: the capital letter L has one square corner, where its two lines meet. So the letter L has 1 right angle.

stepByStep.text: A right angle is a square corner. It measures 90°.
A rectangle has 4 corners, and every one of them is a square corner.
So a rectangle has 4 right angles.

misconceptions.A: Yes! All four corners of a rectangle are square corners.
misconceptions.B: A rectangle has four corners and they all look alike. Check the other two corners as well.
misconceptions.C: Look at the corner of a book or a door. Those are right angles, and a rectangle has them.
misconceptions.D: All the corners of a rectangle are alike. Count every corner.

questionText: How many diagonals does a quadrilateral have?
hints: A diagonal is a line that joins two corners which are not next to each other.
Draw any four-sided shape. From one corner, find the corner that is not joined to it by a side.
Here is a similar idea: a triangle has 3 corners, and every corner is next to the other two. So a triangle has 0 diagonals.

stepByStep.text: A quadrilateral has 4 corners. A diagonal joins two corners that are opposite each other.
The 4 corners make two opposite pairs. Each pair gives one diagonal.
So a quadrilateral has 2 diagonals.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The two pairs of opposite corners give two diagonals.
misconceptions.B: 4 is the number of sides, or of corners. Diagonals join opposite corners, and there are only two such pairs.
misconceptions.C: There is one more. Join the other pair of opposite corners too.
misconceptions.D: Each diagonal uses up two opposite corners. Four corners make only two such pairs.

questionText: If three angles of a quadrilateral are 80°, 90° and 100°, the fourth angle is:
hints: The four angles of any quadrilateral always add up to the same total.
The four angles add up to 360°. Add the three angles you know first.
Here is a similar one: three angles are 70°, 110° and 120°. 70 + 110 + 120 = 300. The fourth angle is 360 − 300 = 60°.

stepByStep.text: The four angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°.
Add the three angles you know.
Take that away from 360.
So the fourth angle is 90°.

misconceptions.B: With 80° the four angles would add up to 350°, not 360°. Find 360 − 270.
misconceptions.C: With 100° the four angles would add up to 370°, not 360°. Find 360 − 270.
misconceptions.D: With 110° the four angles would add up to 380°, not 360°. Find 360 − 270.

questionText: A quadrilateral has all four sides equal, but none of its angles is a right angle. What is it called?
hints: Two of these shapes have four equal sides. What makes them different from each other is their angles.
A square has four equal sides and four right angles. Which shape has four equal sides but leans over, so its angles are not right angles?
A similar one: a quadrilateral with opposite sides equal and four right angles, but with its length different from its breadth, is a rectangle.

stepByStep.text: Four equal sides are found in a square and in a rhombus.
A square always has four right angles, so it does not fit here.
A shape with four equal sides and no right angles is a rhombus.

misconceptions.A: Yes! A rhombus has four equal sides, and its angles need not be right angles.
misconceptions.B: A square does have four equal sides, but all its angles are right angles.
misconceptions.C: A rectangle has four right angles, and only its opposite sides have to be equal.
misconceptions.D: A trapezium has just one pair of parallel sides, and its four sides are not all equal.

questionText: One angle of a parallelogram is 70°. What is the size of the angle next to it?
hints: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal, and two angles that are next to each other add up to 180°.
The angle next to the 70° angle makes 180° together with it. Take 70° away from 180°.
A similar one: if one angle of a parallelogram is 65°, the angle next to it is 180° − 65° = 115°.

stepByStep.text: Angles next to each other in a parallelogram add up to 180°.
Take the known angle away from 180°.
The angle next to it is 110°.

misconceptions.A: 70° is the angle opposite the given one. The angle next to it is different.
misconceptions.B: 20° would be right if the two angles made a right angle. Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram make 180° together.
misconceptions.D: 290° comes from taking 70° from 360°. Two neighbouring angles add up to 180°, and all four add up to 360°.

questionText: The perimeter of a rhombus is 52 cm. How long is each side?
hints: Think about what is special about the sides of a rhombus. The perimeter is all the sides added together.
A rhombus has four equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times one side. Share 52 cm into 4 equal parts.
A similar one: a rhombus with perimeter 36 cm has sides of 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm each.

stepByStep.text: All four sides of a rhombus are equal, so the perimeter is 4 times one side.
Divide the perimeter by 4.
Each side is 13 cm.

misconceptions.A: 26 cm shares the perimeter between 2 sides. A rhombus has 4 equal sides.
misconceptions.C: 48 cm takes 4 away from 52. To share equally among 4 sides, divide by 4.
misconceptions.D: 208 comes from multiplying by 4. A side is shorter than the perimeter, so divide.

questionText: A square handkerchief has sides of 25 cm. Lace is stitched all around its edge. The lace costs ₹3 for every centimetre. What does the lace cost?
hints: Lace that goes all around the edge is as long as the perimeter. Find that length first, then the cost.
A square has 4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times 25 cm.
A similar one: ribbon at ₹2 a centimetre around a square of side 10 cm. The perimeter is 40 cm, so the ribbon costs 40 × 2 = ₹80.

stepByStep.text: Length of lace = perimeter of the square.
Each centimetre costs ₹3.
The lace costs ₹300.

misconceptions.A: ₹75 is the cost of lace for one side only. The lace goes around all four sides.
misconceptions.B: ₹150 is the cost for two sides. A square has four sides.
misconceptions.C: ₹1,875 uses the area, 25 × 25. Lace goes along the edge, so use the perimeter.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 100 cm of lace at ₹3 a centimetre costs ₹300.

questionText: A wire is bent into a square of side 18 cm. The same wire is then bent into a rectangle whose length is twice its breadth. What is the area of the rectangle?
hints: The wire does not change length, so the square and the rectangle have the same perimeter. Use the perimeter to find the sides of the rectangle.
The wire is 4 times 18 cm long. In the rectangle, the length is 2 breadths, so going around it is 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6 breadths.
A similar one: a square of side 6 cm uses 24 cm of wire. For a rectangle with length twice its breadth, 6 breadths make 24 cm, so the breadth is 4 cm, the length is 8 cm and the area is 32 cm².

stepByStep.text: Length of the wire = perimeter of the square.
Around the rectangle there are 6 breadths, because each length is 2 breadths.
The breadth is 12 cm, so the length is twice that.
Area = length times breadth.
The area of the rectangle is 288 cm².

misconceptions.A: 324 cm² is the area of the square. The rectangle has the same perimeter, but a different area.
misconceptions.B: 648 cm² keeps 18 cm as the breadth and doubles it for the length. That rectangle would need more wire than there is.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The rectangle is 24 cm by 12 cm, and 24 × 12 = 288.
misconceptions.D: 72 is the length of the wire in centimetres. Use it to find the sides, then multiply them.

questionText: A rectangular garden is 20 m long and 14 m wide. A path 2 m wide runs all around it on the outside. What is the area of the path?
hints: The garden and the path together make a bigger rectangle. The path is the bigger rectangle with the garden taken out.
The path adds 2 m at both ends of the length and 2 m at both ends of the width. Find the length and width of the big rectangle.
A similar one: a lawn 10 m by 6 m with a 1 m path outside. The big rectangle is 12 m by 8 m, area 96 m². The lawn is 60 m², so the path is 36 m².

stepByStep.text: The path adds 2 m on each side, so 4 m to the length and 4 m to the width.
Area of the garden with the path.
Area of the garden alone.
Area of the path.
The area of the path is 152 m².

misconceptions.B: 72 m² adds the path only once to each measurement. The path is on both sides, so add 4 m, not 2 m.
misconceptions.C: 136 m² is the garden's perimeter times the path's width. That leaves out the four corner squares of the path.
misconceptions.D: 432 m² is the garden and the path together. Take away the garden's own area.

questionText: A floor is 6 m long and 4 m wide. It is covered with square tiles of side 50 cm, with no gaps. How many tiles are needed?
hints: The floor is measured in metres and the tile in centimetres. Use the same unit for both, then count how many tiles fit along the length and along the width.
Two tiles of 50 cm make 1 metre. So how many tiles fit along 6 m, and how many along 4 m?
A similar one: a floor 5 m by 3 m with 50 cm tiles. Ten tiles fit along the length and 6 along the width, so 10 × 6 = 60 tiles are needed.

stepByStep.text: Two tiles of 50 cm make 1 m. Along the 6 m length.
Along the 4 m width.
Tiles needed = tiles in a row times number of rows.
The floor needs 96 tiles.

misconceptions.A: 24 is the area of the floor in square metres. Each square metre holds 4 of these tiles.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 12 tiles along the length and 8 along the width make 96.
misconceptions.C: 48 puts 2 tiles in each square metre. Two tiles fit each way, so 4 tiles cover one square metre.
misconceptions.D: 20 is the perimeter of the floor in metres. Tiles cover the whole floor, so think of rows of tiles.

questionText: A square sheet of paper has sides of 12 cm. It is cut into two equal rectangles by one straight cut. What is the perimeter of each rectangle?
hints: Picture the cut going across the middle of the square. Work out the length and the breadth of one of the pieces.
The cut halves one pair of sides. Each rectangle is 12 cm long. How wide is it?
A similar one: a square of side 10 cm cut into two equal rectangles gives pieces 10 cm by 5 cm. Each has a perimeter of 10 + 5 + 10 + 5 = 30 cm.

stepByStep.text: The cut goes through the middle, so each rectangle is 12 cm long and half of 12 cm wide.
Add the four sides of one rectangle.
The perimeter of each rectangle is 36 cm.

misconceptions.A: 24 cm is half the square's perimeter. Cutting makes a new edge of 12 cm on each piece, so the perimeter is not simply halved.
misconceptions.B: 48 cm is the perimeter of the whole square. Each piece is smaller than that.
misconceptions.C: 72 is the area of each piece, 12 × 6. Perimeter is the distance around.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Each piece is 12 cm by 6 cm, and 12 + 6 + 12 + 6 = 36.

questionText: Think about these four shapes: square, rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram. How many of them always have four right angles?
hints: Go through the shapes one by one. The word always matters: ask whether every shape of that kind must have right angles.
A square and a rectangle have right angles at every corner. Can a rhombus or a parallelogram lean over to one side?
A similar one: how many of the same four shapes always have opposite sides equal? The square, rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram all do, so the count is 4.

stepByStep.text: A square always has four right angles. So does a rectangle.
A rhombus can lean over, like a diamond, so its angles need not be right angles.
A parallelogram can lean over too, so its angles need not be right angles.
Only the square and the rectangle always have four right angles, so the count is 2.

misconceptions.A: The square is one of them, and there is one more: every rectangle has four right angles too.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The square and the rectangle always have four right angles.
misconceptions.C: A rhombus has four equal sides, but it can lean over, so its angles are not always right angles.
misconceptions.D: A rhombus and a parallelogram can both lean over, so they do not always have right angles.

questionText: A rectangle is 20 cm long and 15 cm wide. Its length is made 5 cm longer and its width is made 5 cm shorter. What happens to its area?
hints: Do not guess from the fact that 5 is added and 5 is taken away. Work out the area before and the area after, and compare them.
The new rectangle is 25 cm long and 10 cm wide. Find its area, and the area of the first rectangle.
A similar one: a rectangle 10 cm by 8 cm has area 80 cm². Make it 2 cm longer and 2 cm narrower: 12 cm by 6 cm has area 72 cm². The area decreases by 8 cm².

stepByStep.text: Area at the start.
New length and width.
New area.
Compare the two areas.
The new area is smaller, so it decreases by 50 cm².

misconceptions.A: Yes! The area goes from 300 cm² down to 250 cm².
misconceptions.B: The perimeter stays the same, but the area does not. Work out 25 × 10 and compare it with 20 × 15.
misconceptions.C: The area does change by 50 cm², but the new area, 250 cm², is smaller than the old one, 300 cm².
misconceptions.D: 25 is 5 × 5. Find the two whole areas, 300 cm² and 250 cm², and subtract.

questionText: A hall is 12 m long and 9 m wide. Carpet for the whole floor costs ₹150 for each square metre. A wooden strip along all four walls costs ₹40 for each metre. What is the total cost?
hints: Carpet covers the floor, so it needs the area. A strip along the walls goes around the edge, so it needs the perimeter.
Find the area of the floor with 12 times 9, and the perimeter with 12 + 9 + 12 + 9. Then find each cost separately.
A similar one: a room 5 m by 4 m. Carpet at ₹100 a square metre costs 20 × 100 = ₹2,000. A strip at ₹10 a metre costs 18 × 10 = ₹180. Together that is ₹2,180.

stepByStep.text: Area of the floor, and the cost of the carpet.
Perimeter of the floor, and the cost of the strip.
Add the two costs.
The total cost is ₹17,880.

misconceptions.A: ₹16,200 is the cost of the carpet alone. Add the cost of the wooden strip.
misconceptions.B: ₹20,520 charges both prices on the area. The strip runs along the walls, so it uses the perimeter, 42 m.
misconceptions.C: Yes! ₹16,200 for the carpet and ₹1,680 for the strip make ₹17,880.
misconceptions.D: ₹7,980 charges both prices on the perimeter. Carpet covers the floor, so it uses the area, 108 square metres.

questionText: A rectangular field is 30 m long and 20 m wide. Fence posts are fixed all around it, 5 m apart, with one post at each corner. How many posts are needed?
hints: The posts go around a closed loop. On a closed loop, the number of posts is the same as the number of gaps between them.
Find the perimeter of the field. Then see how many gaps of 5 m fit into it.
A similar one: a square plot of side 10 m with posts 5 m apart. The perimeter is 40 m, so there are 40 ÷ 5 = 8 gaps and 8 posts.

stepByStep.text: Distance around the field.
Number of 5 m gaps around the field.
Around a closed loop every gap ends at a post, and the last gap ends at the first post, so posts and gaps are equal in number.
The field needs 20 posts.

misconceptions.A: 21 adds an extra post, which is right for a straight line of posts. Around a closed loop the last gap comes back to the first post.
misconceptions.B: 24 counts 7 posts on each long side and 5 on each short side, so each corner post is counted twice. Take away the 4 extra.
misconceptions.C: 10 counts the gaps along one long side and one short side only. The posts go all the way around.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 100 m around with posts every 5 m needs 20 posts.

questionText: A wire 40 cm long is bent to make a rectangle. Each side is a whole number of centimetres, and the length is greater than the breadth. What is the difference between the largest area and the smallest area the rectangle can have?
hints: The wire is the perimeter, so the length and the breadth always add up to the same number. Try different pairs and watch how the area changes.
Half of 40 cm is 20 cm, so length + breadth = 20 cm. Start with 19 cm and 1 cm, then 18 cm and 2 cm, and see which way the area moves. Remember the length must stay greater than the breadth.

Similar problem: a 20 cm wire, so length + breadth = 10 cm. The thinnest rectangle is 9 by 1 with area 9 sq cm. The fattest allowed is 6 by 4 with area 24 sq cm, because 5 by 5 has equal sides. The difference is 24 - 9 = 15 sq cm.

stepByStep.text: The length and breadth together are half the wire.
The smallest area comes from the thinnest rectangle, 19 cm by 1 cm.
The area grows as the sides get closer. The closest pair with the length still greater is 11 cm and 9 cm.
Subtract the smallest area from the largest.
So the difference is 80 sq cm.

misconceptions.A: This uses the 10 cm by 10 cm square as the largest. The question says the length is greater than the breadth, so the sides cannot be equal.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The largest is 11 by 9 = 99 sq cm, the smallest is 19 by 1 = 19 sq cm, and 99 - 19 = 80.
misconceptions.C: 99 sq cm is the largest area. The question asks for the difference between the largest and the smallest.
misconceptions.D: 19 sq cm is the smallest area. Now find the largest area and subtract.

questionText: A wire is bent into a square of side 15 cm. The same wire is then bent into a rectangle whose length is 4 cm more than the side of the square. What happens to the area enclosed by the wire?
hints: The wire does not change, so the perimeter stays the same. But the same perimeter does not always enclose the same area. Find both areas and compare.
The perimeter is 4 x 15 cm. If the length becomes 19 cm, work out what the breadth has to be so the perimeter stays the same.

Similar problem: a square of side 10 cm becomes a rectangle 3 cm longer. The length is 13 cm, and since length + breadth must still be 20 cm, the breadth is 7 cm. The area goes from 100 sq cm to 13 x 7 = 91 sq cm, so it decreases by 9 sq cm.

stepByStep.text: The wire is as long as the perimeter of the square.
The length is 19 cm. Length and breadth together are half the wire, so find the breadth.
Find the area of the rectangle.
Compare with the area of the square.
The area becomes smaller.
So the area decreases by 16 sq cm.

misconceptions.A: The perimeter stays the same, but the area does not have to. Work out 15 x 15 and then the area of the new rectangle.
misconceptions.B: This keeps the breadth at 15 cm. The wire is no longer than before, so when the length grows by 4 cm the breadth must shrink by 4 cm.
misconceptions.C: Great work! The rectangle is 19 cm by 11 cm, which is 209 sq cm, and that is 16 sq cm less than 225 sq cm.
misconceptions.D: Good try! The area does get smaller, but find the new breadth first: it is 11 cm, not 15 cm.

questionText: A rectangular park is 30 m long and 20 m wide. Two straight paths, each 2 m wide, run right across the middle of the park. One path runs along the length and the other runs across the width, so they cross each other in the middle. What is the total area covered by the paths?
hints: Each path is a long thin rectangle. Think carefully about the small piece of ground where the two paths cross.
Find the area of the path that is 30 m long, and the area of the path that is 20 m long. Then find the size of the square where they lie on top of each other.
Similar problem: a field 20 m by 10 m with two crossing paths 1 m wide. The paths are 20 sq m and 10 sq m. The crossing square is 1 sq m and belongs to both, so the total is 20 + 10 - 1 = 29 sq m.

stepByStep.text: Find the area of the path along the length.
Find the area of the path across the width.
Where they cross, a square of side 2 m belongs to both paths.
Add the two paths and take the crossing square away once.
So the paths cover 96 sq m.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The paths are 60 sq m and 40 sq m, and the 4 sq m square where they cross is counted only once.
misconceptions.B: This adds 60 and 40. The little square where the paths cross is part of both, so it has been counted twice.
misconceptions.C: The crossing square should be taken away, not added. It is already inside both paths.
misconceptions.D: This is the area of the park that is left as grass. The question asks for the area of the paths.

questionText: A square garden has a path 1 m wide all around it on the outside. The area of the path is 40 sq m. How long is each side of the garden?
hints: The path is made of four strips along the sides of the garden and four little squares at the corners. Work backwards from the area of the path.
Each corner piece is a square of side 1 m. Take the four corner squares away from 40 sq m first, and see what is left for the four strips.
Similar problem: the path has area 24 sq m. The four corners take 4 sq m, leaving 20 sq m for four strips. Each strip is 5 sq m and 1 m wide, so it is 5 m long. The garden has sides of 5 m.

stepByStep.text: The four corners of the path are squares of side 1 m.
Take the corners away to find the area of the four strips.
Each strip has the same area.
A strip of 9 sq m that is 1 m wide is 9 m long, as long as a side of the garden.
So each side of the garden is 9 m.

misconceptions.A: This shares all 40 sq m among four strips. The four corner squares of the path are also part of the 40 sq m.
misconceptions.B: Try it: a garden of side 8 m with this path makes a 10 m square outside. 100 - 64 is 36 sq m, a little too small.
misconceptions.C: Try it: a garden of side 11 m makes a 13 m square outside. 169 - 121 is 48 sq m, which is too big.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The big square is 11 m, the garden is 9 m, and 121 - 81 = 40.

questionText: A rectangle has an area of 24 sq cm. Its length is made 2 times as long and its breadth is made 3 times as long. What is the area of the new rectangle?
hints: You are not told the length or the breadth. Choose any pair that gives the right area and see what happens. Then try another pair to check.
Try a rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm. Make the length 2 times as long and the breadth 3 times as long, then multiply.
Similar problem: a rectangle of area 5 sq cm, say 5 cm by 1 cm. Make the length 3 times and the breadth 2 times as long: 15 cm by 2 cm. The new area is 30 sq cm, which is 6 times the old area.

stepByStep.text: Pick a rectangle with area 24 sq cm, such as 6 cm by 4 cm.
Make the length 2 times as long and the breadth 3 times as long.
Find the new area.
The area has been multiplied by 2 and then by 3, which is 6 times. This is true for any rectangle of area 24 sq cm.
So the area of the new rectangle is 144 sq cm.

misconceptions.A: This multiplies the area by 2 + 3. Making both sides longer multiplies the area twice over: by 2 and then by 3.
misconceptions.B: This only doubles the area. The breadth has also been made 3 times as long.
misconceptions.C: Lovely! The area becomes 2 x 3 = 6 times as big, and 24 x 6 = 144.
misconceptions.D: This only triples the area. The length has also been made 2 times as long.

questionText: A rectangle is drawn on paper. If its length were made 3 cm longer, with the breadth unchanged, its area would grow by 21 sq cm. If instead its breadth were made 2 cm longer, with the length unchanged, its area would grow by 20 sq cm. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
hints: When one side of a rectangle grows, the extra area is a thin strip. Think about the two sides of that strip.
The first strip is 3 cm one way and as long as the breadth the other way, and its area is 21 sq cm. Use this to find the breadth.

Similar problem: making the length 2 cm longer adds 10 sq cm, so the breadth is 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm. Making the breadth 4 cm longer adds 32 sq cm, so the length is 32 ÷ 4 = 8 cm. The perimeter is 2 x (8 + 5) = 26 cm.

stepByStep.text: The first extra strip is 3 cm by the breadth.
The second extra strip is 2 cm by the length.
So the rectangle is 10 cm long and 7 cm wide.
Find the perimeter.
So the perimeter of the rectangle is 34 cm.

misconceptions.A: Excellent! The breadth is 7 cm, the length is 10 cm, and 2 x (10 + 7) = 34.
misconceptions.B: This is the length plus the breadth. A perimeter goes all the way round, so there are two lengths and two breadths.
misconceptions.C: This adds the two extra areas. Use each extra area to find one side of the rectangle instead.
misconceptions.D: This doubles once too often. The sides are 10 cm and 7 cm, so add them and double once.

questionText: Rahul has 36 square tiles, each of side 1 cm. He lays all 36 tiles flat, with no gaps, to make one rectangle. A square counts as a rectangle here, and a 4 by 9 rectangle is the same as a 9 by 4 rectangle. How many different rectangles can he make?
hints: The number of tiles is the area of the rectangle. Each rectangle is a pair of whole numbers that multiply to give that area.
List the pairs in order: 1 by something, 2 by something, 3 by something, and stop when the pairs begin to repeat the other way round.
Similar problem: 16 tiles. The pairs are 1 by 16, 2 by 8 and 4 by 4. After that, 8 by 2 is a repeat. So 16 tiles make 3 different rectangles, even though 16 has more factors than that.

stepByStep.text: Each rectangle uses all 36 tiles, so its two sides multiply to give 36.
List the pairs in order.
After 6 by 6 the pairs repeat the other way round, such as 9 by 4.
Count the pairs: 1 by 36, 2 by 18, 3 by 12, 4 by 9 and 6 by 6.
So Rahul can make 5 different rectangles.

misconceptions.A: Great job! The pairs are 1 by 36, 2 by 18, 3 by 12, 4 by 9 and 6 by 6, which makes 5.
misconceptions.B: This is the number of factors of 36. Each rectangle uses two factors as a pair, and 6 pairs with itself.
misconceptions.C: Almost! The 6 by 6 square counts as a rectangle here, so add it to your list.
misconceptions.D: Check your list for a repeat, such as 4 by 9 and 9 by 4. They are the same rectangle turned round.

questionText: A big square is divided by straight lines into 3 rows of 3 equal small squares, like a noughts and crosses board. How many squares of all sizes are there in the drawing?
hints: The small squares are not the only squares. Bigger squares can be made from blocks of small squares, and those bigger squares can overlap each other.
Count by size: first the squares made of 1 small square, then those made of a 2 by 2 block, then the 3 by 3 block. For the 2 by 2 blocks, think about where the top left corner can be.
Similar problem: a square divided into 2 rows of 2 small squares. There are 4 small squares and 1 big square, so there are 5 squares of all sizes.

stepByStep.text: Count the small squares.
Count the squares made of a 2 by 2 block. Such a block can start in 2 places across and 2 places down.
There is 1 square made of the whole 3 by 3 block.
Add them all.
So there are 14 squares of all sizes.

misconceptions.A: These are the small squares only. Look for bigger squares made from blocks of four small squares, and the whole board too.
misconceptions.B: This adds the big outline to the 9 small squares. There are also squares made from 2 by 2 blocks. How many of those can you find?
misconceptions.C: So close! You may have missed one of the 2 by 2 blocks, or the whole board itself.
misconceptions.D: Wonderful! 9 small squares, 4 squares of side 2 and 1 big square make 14.

questionText: Five equal small squares are joined side by side in one straight row to make a long strip. Look at every shape made of one small square or of several neighbouring small squares. How many of these shapes are rectangles that are NOT squares?
hints: Count by length: shapes that are 2 squares long, 3 squares long, and so on. Shapes of the same length can overlap. Think about which shapes are squares.
A shape 2 squares long can start at the 1st, 2nd, 3rd or 4th small square. Count those, then do the same for shapes 3, 4 and 5 squares long.

Similar problem: a strip of 3 small squares. Shapes 2 squares long: 2 of them. Shapes 3 squares long: 1. The single small squares are squares, so they are left out. That gives 2 + 1 = 3 rectangles that are not squares.

stepByStep.text: A shape made of just 1 small square is a square, so it is not counted.
Shapes 2 squares long: 4 of them. Shapes 3 squares long: 3 of them.
Shapes 4 squares long: 2 of them. The whole strip, 5 squares long: 1.
Add them.
So 10 of the shapes are rectangles that are not squares.

misconceptions.A: Well counted! 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 shapes are longer than they are tall.
misconceptions.B: This counts every shape, including the 5 single small squares. The question asks for the ones that are not squares.
misconceptions.C: These are the 5 single small squares, which are squares. Count the longer shapes instead.
misconceptions.D: These are only the shapes 2 squares long. Shapes that are 3, 4 and 5 squares long are rectangles too.

questionText: Which of these statements about quadrilaterals is true?

options.text: A quadrilateral with four equal sides is always a square
A quadrilateral with four right angles always has four equal sides
A quadrilateral with two pairs of equal sides is always a parallelogram
A quadrilateral with four equal sides always has its opposite sides parallel

hints: A statement with the word 'always' is true only if no shape at all breaks it. For each statement, try to think of one quadrilateral that breaks it.
Think about a rhombus that leans over, a long rectangle and a kite. Test each statement on these three shapes.

Similar problem: is 'a quadrilateral with four right angles is always a square' true? A rectangle 5 cm by 2 cm has four right angles, but its sides are not all equal. One shape that breaks the statement is enough, so it is not always true.

stepByStep.text: A leaning rhombus has four equal sides but no right angles, so four equal sides do not always make a square.
A long rectangle has four right angles but its sides are not all equal.
A kite has two pairs of equal sides, but the equal sides are next to each other, and it is not a parallelogram.
A quadrilateral with four equal sides is a rhombus, or a square, which is a special rhombus. In every rhombus the opposite sides are parallel.
So the true statement is: a quadrilateral with four equal sides always has its opposite sides parallel.

misconceptions.A: Think of a rhombus that leans to one side. Its four sides are equal, but its angles are not right angles.
misconceptions.B: Think of a rectangle 6 cm long and 2 cm wide. It has four right angles. Are its four sides equal?
misconceptions.C: This sounds right, but think of a kite. It has two pairs of equal sides, and they sit next to each other, so no sides are parallel.
misconceptions.D: Well reasoned! Four equal sides make a rhombus, and in every rhombus the opposite sides are parallel.

questionText: The four angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°. Which of these can a quadrilateral NOT have?

options.text: Two right angles and one acute angle

hints: Use the total of 360°. For each choice, either find four angles that fit and add up to 360°, or explain why the total can never be reached.
Start with three obtuse angles: try 100°, 100° and 100°, and see what is left for the fourth angle. Then think about four angles that are each less than 90°.

Similar problem: can a triangle have three acute angles? Yes: 60°, 60° and 60° add up to 180°. Can a triangle have two right angles? No: 90° + 90° already makes 180°, leaving nothing for the third angle.

stepByStep.text: A square has four right angles, so four right angles are possible.
Three obtuse angles are possible: 100°, 100°, 100° and 60°.
Two right angles and one acute angle are possible: 90°, 90°, 80° and 100°.
Four acute angles are each less than 90°, so together they are less than 360°.
So a quadrilateral cannot have four acute angles.

misconceptions.A: A square and a rectangle both have four right angles, so this is possible.
misconceptions.B: This feels impossible, but try 100°, 100°, 100° and 60°. They add up to 360°.
misconceptions.C: Brilliant! Four angles that are each less than 90° can never add up to 360°.
misconceptions.D: Try 90°, 90°, 80° and 100°. They add up to 360°, so this is possible.

questionText: A square sheet of paper is cut into 4 equal rectangular strips by three straight cuts, all parallel to one side of the square. Each strip has a perimeter of 40 cm. What is the area of the square sheet?
hints: Picture one strip. Its long side is a whole side of the square, and its short side is one quarter of a side. Work backwards from the perimeter of a strip.
Half of the strip's perimeter is one long side plus one short side, which is 20 cm. The long side is 4 times the short side.

Similar problem: a square is cut into 2 equal rectangles, each with perimeter 18 cm. Long side + short side = 9 cm, and the long side is 2 times the short side, so they are 6 cm and 3 cm. The square has side 6 cm and area 36 sq cm.

stepByStep.text: Half the perimeter of a strip is its long side plus its short side.
The long side is 4 times the short side, so 20 cm is 5 equal parts.
The long side of a strip is the side of the square.
Find the area of the square.
So the area of the square sheet is 256 sq cm.

misconceptions.A: This adds up the four strip perimeters and treats 160 cm as the perimeter of the square. The cut edges are inside the square, so they are not part of its perimeter.
misconceptions.B: Exactly! Each strip is 16 cm by 4 cm, so the square has side 16 cm and area 256 sq cm.
misconceptions.C: This treats a strip as a square of side 10 cm. A strip is long and thin: its long side is 4 times its short side.
misconceptions.D: This takes 20 cm as the side of the square. But 20 cm is the long side and the short side of a strip together.

questionText: The length of a rectangle is 3 times its breadth. Both are whole numbers of centimetres. Which of these can be the area of the rectangle?
hints: If the breadth is some number, the length is 3 times that number. Think about what the area must then look like.
The area is 3 x breadth x breadth. So divide each area by 3 and ask: is the result a number multiplied by itself?

Similar problem: the length is 2 times the breadth. Then the area is 2 x breadth x breadth. An area of 50 sq cm works, because 50 ÷ 2 = 25 = 5 x 5, giving a rectangle 10 cm by 5 cm. An area of 40 sq cm does not, because 40 ÷ 2 = 20 is not a number times itself.

stepByStep.text: The area is length x breadth, which is 3 x breadth x breadth.
Divide each area by 3.
Only 25 is a number multiplied by itself.
So the breadth is 5 cm and the length is 15 cm.
So the area can be 75 sq cm.

misconceptions.A: 54 ÷ 3 = 18, and 18 is not a whole number multiplied by itself, so no whole-number breadth fits.
misconceptions.B: 36 is 3 x 12, but 12 is not a whole number multiplied by itself. A 6 by 6 square has this area, but its length is not 3 times its breadth.
misconceptions.C: 96 ÷ 3 = 32, and 32 is not a whole number multiplied by itself, so no whole-number breadth fits.
misconceptions.D: Yes! A rectangle 15 cm by 5 cm has a length 3 times its breadth and an area of 75 sq cm.

questionText: A square sheet of card has sides of 10 cm. A small square of side 4 cm is cut away from one corner of the sheet. What is the perimeter of the card that is left?
hints: Cutting a piece away makes the area smaller, but the perimeter is a different thing. Walk around the edge of the new shape and add up every edge, including the new ones.
The new shape has six edges. Two of the old edges are now 4 cm shorter, and there are two new edges inside the notch. Find the length of each.

Similar problem: a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm with a 2 cm square cut from one corner. The edges are 8, 5, 6, 3 and two new edges of 2 cm each. They add up to 26 cm, the same as the perimeter of the whole rectangle.

stepByStep.text: Two edges of the card are still 10 cm long.
The two edges that met at the cut corner are now shorter.
The notch adds two new edges of 4 cm each.
Add all six edges.
So the perimeter of the card that is left is 40 cm.

misconceptions.A: This takes away all four sides of the small square. Only two of its sides were on the edge of the card, and the cut makes two new edges.
misconceptions.B: Well spotted! The two new edges of the notch exactly make up for the two pieces removed, so the perimeter is still 40 cm.
misconceptions.C: This takes away the two 4 cm pieces that were removed, but the notch also has two new 4 cm edges on the inside. Add those back.
misconceptions.D: This adds 8 cm for the new edges but forgets that two old edges each became 4 cm shorter.

questionText: Find the area of a rectangle with length 26 cm and breadth 20 cm.
hints: This asks for the area of a rectangle, which is the space inside it. Area is found by multiplying, not adding.
Multiply the length by the breadth. To multiply 26 by 20, you can work out 26 × 2 first and then make it ten times bigger.
Similar example: a rectangle is 15 cm long and 30 cm broad. Its area is 15 × 30. Since 15 × 3 = 45, ten times that is 450, so the area is 450 square cm.

stepByStep.text: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth, so multiply 26 by 20.
26 × 2 = 52, and 26 × 20 is ten times that.
The area is 520 square cm.

misconceptions.A: 92 is the perimeter, 2 × 46. Area is the space inside, so multiply the length by the breadth.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 26 × 20 = 520, so the area is 520 square cm.
misconceptions.C: 1040 is double the area. For area, multiply 26 by 20 just once.
misconceptions.D: 46 is 26 + 20. For area, multiply the length by the breadth instead of adding.

questionText: Find the perimeter of a rectangle with length 14 cm and breadth 7 cm.
hints: Perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape. A rectangle has two lengths and two breadths.
Add the length and the breadth, 14 and 7, to get halfway round. Then think about how to get all the way round.
Similar example: a rectangle is 9 cm long and 4 cm broad. Length plus breadth is 9 + 4 = 13, and all the way round is 2 × 13 = 26 cm.

stepByStep.text: Add the length and the breadth. This takes you halfway round the rectangle.
There are two lengths and two breadths, so double it.
The perimeter is 42 cm.

misconceptions.A: 98 is 14 × 7, which is the area. Perimeter is the distance around, so add the sides.
misconceptions.B: 56 is 4 × 14, as if all four sides were 14 cm. Two sides are 14 cm and two are 7 cm.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 14 + 7 = 21, and twice 21 is 42.
misconceptions.D: 21 is one length plus one breadth, which is only halfway round. Double it.

questionText: Find the perimeter of a rectangle with length 21 cm and breadth 20 cm.
hints: Perimeter is the total distance around the rectangle. You walk along two lengths and two breadths.
Start by adding one length and one breadth, 21 and 20. Then remember that each of them appears twice.
Similar example: a rectangle is 12 cm long and 10 cm broad. One length and one breadth make 12 + 10 = 22, and the whole way round is 2 × 22 = 44 cm.

stepByStep.text: Add one length and one breadth.
The rectangle has two lengths and two breadths, so double 41.
The perimeter is 82 cm.

misconceptions.A: 420 is 21 × 20, which is the area. Perimeter is the distance around, so add the sides.
misconceptions.B: 41 is one length plus one breadth, which is only halfway round. Double it.
misconceptions.C: 84 is 4 × 21, as if all four sides were 21 cm. Two sides are 21 cm and two are 20 cm.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 21 + 20 = 41, and twice 41 is 82.

questionText: Find the area of a rectangle with length 13 cm and breadth 6 cm.
hints: Area is the space inside the rectangle. It is found by multiplying the two side lengths.
Multiply the length by the breadth. You can split 13 into 10 and 3 and multiply each part by 6.
Similar example: a rectangle is 14 cm long and 5 cm broad. 10 × 5 = 50 and 4 × 5 = 20, so 14 × 5 = 70. The area is 70 square cm.

stepByStep.text: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth, so multiply 13 by 6.
The area is 78 square cm.

misconceptions.A: 19 is 13 + 6. For area, multiply the length by the breadth instead of adding.
misconceptions.B: 38 is the perimeter, 2 × 19. Area is the space inside, so multiply 13 by 6.
misconceptions.C: 156 is double the area. For area, multiply 13 by 6 just once.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 13 × 6 = 78, so the area is 78 square cm.

questionText: Find the perimeter of a rectangle with length 7 cm and breadth 3 cm.
hints: Perimeter means the distance around the outside of the shape. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two breadths.
Add the length and the breadth, 7 and 3. That is the distance along two sides, so think about the other two sides as well.
Similar example: a rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm broad. Two sides together are 8 + 5 = 13 cm, and all four sides are 2 × 13 = 26 cm.

stepByStep.text: Add the length and the breadth.
That covers two of the four sides. The other two sides are the same, so double it.
The perimeter is 20 cm.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 7 + 3 = 10, and twice 10 is 20.
misconceptions.B: 10 is one length plus one breadth, which is only halfway round. Double it.
misconceptions.C: 21 is 7 × 3, which is the area. Perimeter is the distance around, so add the sides.
misconceptions.D: 28 is 4 × 7, as if all four sides were 7 cm. Two sides are 7 cm and two are 3 cm.

questionText: Find the area of a rectangle with length 24 cm and breadth 12 cm.
hints: The area of a rectangle tells you how much flat space it covers. You find it by multiplying, not by adding the sides.
Multiply the length by the breadth. You can split 12 into 10 and 2 and multiply 24 by each part.
Similar example: a rectangle is 21 cm long and 13 cm broad. 21 × 10 = 210 and 21 × 3 = 63, so the area is 210 + 63 = 273 square cm.

stepByStep.text: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth, so multiply 24 by 12.
So 24 × 12 = 288, and the area is 288 square cm.

misconceptions.A: 576 is double the area. For area, multiply 24 by 12 just once.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 24 × 12 = 288, so the area is 288 square cm.
misconceptions.C: 72 is the perimeter, 2 × 36. Area is the space inside, so multiply 24 by 12.
misconceptions.D: 36 is 24 + 12. For area, multiply the length by the breadth instead of adding.

questionText: A rectangle of length 4 cm and breadth 1 cm is cut into 4 equal squares. By how much is the sum of the perimeters of the 4 squares more than the perimeter of the rectangle?
hints: Find two things: the perimeter of the rectangle, and the total of the perimeters of all the squares. Then compare them.
Each square has side 1 cm. Find the perimeter of one square, then of all 4 squares together. Find the perimeter of the 4 cm by 1 cm rectangle too.

Similar example: a 3 cm by 1 cm rectangle is cut into 3 squares of side 1 cm. The squares have 3 × 4 = 12 cm of perimeter in all. The rectangle has 2 × (3 + 1) = 8 cm. The difference is 12 − 8 = 4 cm.

stepByStep.text: Each square has side 1 cm, so its perimeter is 4 cm.
Add up the four squares.
Find the perimeter of the rectangle.
Subtract. The squares have 6 cm more.

misconceptions.A: 4 cm is the perimeter of just one square. Add up all 4 squares, then compare with the rectangle.
