misconceptions.A: This is 8 × 3. For area, multiply the side by itself: 8 × 8.
misconceptions.B: This is 8 too many, like one extra row. Work out 8 × 8 once more.
misconceptions.C: This is double the area. Multiply the side by itself just once.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 8 × 8 = 64, so the area is 64 cm².

questionText: The area of a square with side 9 m is:
hints: Area is the space inside the square. Look at both the number and the unit in each choice, because area is measured in square units.
Multiply the side by itself. Then choose the unit that goes with area.
Similar example: a square has a side of 7 m. Its area is 7 × 7 = 49 square metres, written 49 sq. m.

stepByStep.text: The area of a square is side times side.
The side is in metres, so the area is in square metres, written sq. m. The unit m on its own measures length, not area.
The area is 81 sq. m.

misconceptions.A: 18 comes from 9 × 2. For area, multiply the side by itself: 9 × 9.
misconceptions.B: The number 81 is right, but area is measured in square metres, not metres.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 9 × 9 = 81, and area is measured in square metres.
misconceptions.D: 36 m is the perimeter, 4 × 9. Area is side times side, in square metres.

questionText: A rectangle has length 12 cm and breadth 7 cm. Its perimeter is:
hints: Perimeter is the distance all the way around. A rectangle has two lengths and two breadths, and the answer is a length, not an area.
Add the length and the breadth, 12 and 7. That is halfway round, so think about what to do next.
Similar example: a rectangle has length 15 cm and breadth 6 cm. Length plus breadth is 15 + 6 = 21 cm, and the perimeter is 2 × 21 = 42 cm.

stepByStep.text: Add the length and the breadth.
The rectangle has two lengths and two breadths, so double 19.
The perimeter is 38 cm.

misconceptions.A: 19 cm is one length plus one breadth, which is only halfway round. Double it.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 12 + 7 = 19, and twice 19 is 38.
misconceptions.C: 84 comes from 12 × 7, which is the area. Perimeter is the distance around, so add the sides.
misconceptions.D: 48 cm is 4 × 12, as if all four sides were 12 cm. Two sides are 12 cm and two are 7 cm.

questionText: A rectangle has length 15 cm and breadth 8 cm. Its area is:
hints: Area is the space inside the rectangle. It is found by multiplying the length by the breadth.
Multiply 15 by 8. You can split 15 into 10 and 5 and multiply each part by 8.
Similar example: a rectangle has length 12 cm and breadth 9 cm. 10 × 9 = 90 and 2 × 9 = 18, so the area is 90 + 18 = 108 square cm.

stepByStep.text: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth, so multiply 15 by 8.
The area is 120 cm².

misconceptions.A: 80 is only 10 × 8. The length is 15, so add 5 × 8 as well.
misconceptions.B: 23 is 15 + 8. For area, multiply the length by the breadth instead of adding.
misconceptions.C: 46 is the perimeter, 2 × 23. Area is the space inside, so multiply 15 by 8.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 15 × 8 = 120, so the area is 120 square cm.

questionText: A rectangle is 6 cm long and 3 cm wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length × width. Set up 6 × 3 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 12 cm long and 5 cm wide. Area = 12 × 5 = 60 cm².

stepByStep.text: The area of a rectangle is length × width.
6 × 3 means 6 groups of 3. Add them up.
So the area is 18 cm².

misconceptions.A: This is 6 too many, like one extra row. Work out 6 × 3 once more.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 6 × 3 = 18, so the area is 18 cm².
misconceptions.C: This is 6 + 3. For area you multiply the length by the width.
misconceptions.D: Check this by multiplying 6 × 3 again. The area must match that product.

questionText: Find the side of a square whose perimeter is numerically equal to its area.
hints: For a square, the perimeter is 4 times the side and the area is the side times the side. You need a side for which these two numbers come out the same.
Test the sides offered in the choices. For each one, work out 4 times the side and the side times itself, and compare the two results.

Similar example: is the perimeter of a square of side 5 equal in number to its area? The perimeter is 4 × 5 = 20 and the area is 5 × 5 = 25. They are not equal, so 5 is not such a side. Test other sides in the same way.

stepByStep.text: The perimeter of a square is 4 times the side, and the area is the side times the side. Test each side that is offered.
Side 8: the perimeter is 4 × 8 = 32 and the area is 8 × 8 = 64. These are not equal.
Side 6: the perimeter is 4 × 6 = 24 and the area is 6 × 6 = 36. These are not equal.
Side 4: the perimeter is 16 and the area is also 16. These are equal.
The side of the square is 4.

misconceptions.A: For a side of 8 the perimeter is 32 but the area is 64. Try a smaller side.
misconceptions.B: For a side of 6 the perimeter is 24 but the area is 36. Try a smaller side.
misconceptions.C: Yes! With a side of 4, the perimeter is 16 and the area is also 16.
misconceptions.D: It can be found by testing. Work out 4 times the side and the side times itself for each side offered.

questionText: A rectangle is 14 cm long and 6 cm wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length × width. Set up 14 × 6 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 11 cm long and 7 cm wide. Area = 11 × 7 = 77 cm².

stepByStep.text: The area of a rectangle is length × width.
Split 14 into 10 and 4. Multiply the 10 by 6.
Now multiply the 4 by 6.
Add the two parts. So the area is 84 cm².

misconceptions.A: This is half of the area. Multiply the full length by the full width.
misconceptions.B: This is 14 too many, like one extra row. Work out 14 × 6 once more.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 14 × 6 = 84, so the area is 84 cm².
misconceptions.D: This is 14 + 6. For area you multiply the length by the width.

questionText: A rectangle is 13 cm long and 3 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the rectangle. Remember that a rectangle has two lengths and two widths.
Add the length and the width first: 13 + 3. Then think about how many of each side there are.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 9 cm long and 5 cm wide. 9 + 5 = 14. Double it: 14 × 2 = 28 cm.

stepByStep.text: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. Start by adding the length and the width.
There are two lengths and two widths, so double it. The perimeter is 32 cm.

misconceptions.A: This is 13 + 3, just one length and one width. There are two of each, so double it.
misconceptions.B: This counts the length three times. Use two lengths and two widths only.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 13 + 3 = 16, and double that is 32 cm.
misconceptions.D: This is 13 × 3, which gives the area. For perimeter, add up all four sides.

questionText: Which of the following can be the length and breadth of a rectangle whose perimeter is 32 m?
hints: The perimeter is two lengths and two breadths. So first work out what one length and one breadth must add up to.
Halve the perimeter, 32 m. Then add the two numbers in each choice and see which pair gives that half.
Similar example: a rectangle has a perimeter of 20 m, so length plus breadth is 20 ÷ 2 = 10 m. The pair 6.5 m and 3.5 m fits, because 6.5 + 3.5 = 10.

stepByStep.text: Half the perimeter is one length plus one breadth.
Test 18 m and 14 m: 18 + 14 = 32. That is the whole perimeter, not half of it, so this pair is too big.
Test 8 m and 7 m: 8 + 7 = 15, which is 1 short of 16.
Test 10.5 m and 5.5 m. They add to 16, so this pair fits.
The length and breadth can be 10.5 m, 5.5 m.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 10.5 + 5.5 = 16, and twice 16 is 32.
misconceptions.B: 18 and 14 add to 32, but that is only one length and one breadth. Their perimeter would be 64 m.
misconceptions.C: 8 and 7 add to 15, which gives a perimeter of 30 m. Length plus breadth must be 16.
misconceptions.D: One of the pairs does fit. Halve 32 to get 16, and look for the pair that adds to 16.

questionText: A rectangle is 19 cm long and 16 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the rectangle. Remember that a rectangle has two lengths and two widths.
Add the length and the width first: 19 + 16. Then think about how many of each side there are.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 20 cm long and 6 cm wide. 20 + 6 = 26. Double it: 26 × 2 = 52 cm.

stepByStep.text: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. Start by adding the length and the width.
There are two lengths and two widths, so double it. The perimeter is 70 cm.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 19 + 16 = 35, and double that is 70 cm.
misconceptions.B: This is close, but 7 too many. Add 19 and 16 again, then double the total.
misconceptions.C: This counts the length three times. Use two lengths and two widths only.
misconceptions.D: This is 19 + 16, just one length and one width. There are two of each, so double it.

questionText: Find the perimeter of a rectangle whose length is (2m + 5n) and breadth is (m − 3n).
hints: The perimeter of a rectangle is the distance all the way round it: two lengths and two breadths. Here the sides are written with letters, so add like terms together, m with m and n with n.
First add the length and the breadth: (2m + 5n) + (m − 3n). Collect the m terms, then the n terms, taking care with the minus sign.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle has length (3p + 4q) and breadth (p − q). For length plus breadth, 3p + p = 4p and 4q − q = 3q, which gives 4p + 3q. The perimeter is twice this, 8p + 6q.

stepByStep.text: The perimeter is twice the sum of the length and the breadth.
Add the m terms: 2m + m = 3m. Add the n terms: 5n − 3n = 2n. So length plus breadth is 3m + 2n.
Double both parts: 2 × 3m = 6m and 2 × 2n = 4n.
The perimeter is 6m + 4n.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Length plus breadth is 3m + 2n, and doubling it gives 6m + 4n.
misconceptions.B: 3m − 2n is nearly the length plus the breadth, but 5n − 3n = 2n, so the 2n is added, not taken away. A perimeter also needs two lengths and two breadths.
misconceptions.C: 12m + 8n is 4 × (3m + 2n). A rectangle has two lengths and two breadths, so the sum of the length and breadth is only doubled.
misconceptions.D: In 6m + 2n the 3m was doubled but the 2n was not. Both parts of 3m + 2n must be multiplied by 2.

questionText: The length and breadth of a rectangle are (3a − 5) cm and (a + 5) cm. If the perimeter is 40 cm, find a.
hints: The perimeter is twice the sum of the length and the breadth. Write that sum using a, and then see what a must be to make the perimeter 40 cm.
Add the length and the breadth: (3a − 5) + (a + 5). Notice what happens to the − 5 and the + 5.

Here is a similar one: the sides are (2b − 3) cm and (b + 3) cm and the perimeter is 36 cm. Length plus breadth is 3b, because − 3 and + 3 cancel. The perimeter is twice that, 6b, so 6 × b = 36 and b = 36 ÷ 6 = 6.

stepByStep.text: Add the length and the breadth. 3a + a = 4a, and the − 5 and + 5 cancel each other, so the sum is 4a.
The perimeter is two lengths and two breadths, so it is twice 4a, which is 8a. Take care not to stop at 4a.
The perimeter is 40 cm, so 8 × a = 40. That gives a = 40 ÷ 8 = 5.
Check: the length is 3 × 5 − 5 = 10 cm and the breadth is 5 + 5 = 10 cm, and 2 × (10 + 10) = 40 cm. So a is 5.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The perimeter is 8a, and 8 × 5 = 40.
misconceptions.B: If a were 4, the sides would be 7 cm and 9 cm, and the perimeter would be 2 × 16 = 32 cm. Try the sum of the sides again.
misconceptions.C: 8 is the number of a's in the perimeter, since the perimeter is 8a. The question asks for the value of one a.
misconceptions.D: 10 comes from 40 ÷ 4, using only one length and one breadth. The perimeter has two lengths and two breadths.

questionText: Sam ran ten rounds around a rectangular field. The field is 350 m long and 120 m wide. What total distance did Sam run?
hints: One round of the field is its perimeter. Find the distance for one round first, then for all the rounds, and check the units in the choices.
Add the length and the width, 350 m and 120 m, and double the total to get one round.
Similar example: a field is 200 m long and 150 m wide. One round is 2 × (200 + 150) = 700 m. Five rounds are 5 × 700 = 3500 m. Since 1000 m is 1 km, that is 3.5 km.

stepByStep.text: Add the length and the width of the field.
Double it to get one full round of the field.
Sam ran ten rounds, so multiply one round by 10.
The distance is 9400 m. Since 1000 m is 1 km, divide by 1000 to change it to kilometres.
Sam ran 9.4 km.

misconceptions.A: 940 m is one round. Sam ran ten rounds, so multiply by 10.
misconceptions.B: 4700 m is ten times 470 m, but 470 m is only one length plus one width. One full round is double that.
misconceptions.C: Yes! One round is 940 m, ten rounds are 9400 m, and that is 9.4 km.
misconceptions.D: 4.7 km uses 470 m for one round. A full round has two lengths and two widths, which is 940 m.

questionText: The length and breadth of a rectangle add up to 12 cm and they differ by 2 cm. Find the area.
hints: Before you can find the area you need the length and the breadth. You know their sum and their difference, so find the two numbers first.
Look for two numbers that add up to 12 and are 2 apart. One way is to take the difference away from the sum and halve what is left, which gives the smaller number.

Similar example: the length and breadth add up to 14 cm and differ by 2 cm. Taking 2 from 14 leaves 12, and half of 12 is 6, so the breadth is 6 cm and the length is 6 + 2 = 8 cm. The area is 8 × 6 = 48 square cm.

stepByStep.text: Take the difference from the sum. What is left is two breadths.
Halve it to get the breadth.
The length is 2 cm more than the breadth.
Check that 7 + 5 = 12. Now multiply the length by the breadth to get the area.
The area is 35 cm².

misconceptions.A: 24 comes from 12 × 2, but 12 and 2 are the sum and the difference, not the sides. Find the length and the breadth first.
misconceptions.B: 30 is 6 × 5, but 6 and 5 are only 1 apart. The sides must add to 12 and be 2 apart.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The sides are 7 cm and 5 cm, and 7 × 5 = 35.
misconceptions.D: Check both the sides and the unit. The sides are two numbers that add to 12 and differ by 2, and area is measured in square cm.

questionText: Each side of a square is 9 cm long. What is the perimeter of the square?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the square. All four sides are the same length.
A square has 4 equal sides. So you need 4 lots of 9 cm.
Here is a similar one: a square with side 7 cm. Perimeter = 4 × 7 = 28 cm.

stepByStep.text: A square has 4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 × side.
4 × 9 means 4 groups of 9. Add them up.
So the perimeter is 36 cm.

misconceptions.A: This counts five sides. A square has only four sides.
misconceptions.B: This counts only three sides. A square has four sides.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 4 × 9 = 36, so the perimeter is 36 cm.
misconceptions.D: This is double the perimeter. Go round the four sides just once.

questionText: Which of the following has the LEAST perimeter?

options.text: an equilateral triangle of side 6 cm
a rectangle with dimensions 5 cm and 3 cm

hints: Perimeter is the distance around a shape. Find the perimeter of each of the four shapes, then compare them.
Count the sides of each shape. A square and a rhombus each have 4 equal sides, an equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides, and a rectangle has two lengths and two breadths.

Similar example: compare an equilateral triangle of side 9 cm with a square of side 7 cm. The triangle's perimeter is 3 × 9 = 27 cm and the square's is 4 × 7 = 28 cm. The triangle has the smaller perimeter, even though its side is longer.

stepByStep.text: The square has 4 sides of 5.5 cm, so its perimeter is 22 cm.
The equilateral triangle has 3 sides of 6 cm, so its perimeter is 18 cm.
The rectangle has two sides of 5 cm and two sides of 3 cm, so its perimeter is 16 cm.
The rhombus has 4 sides of 5 cm, so its perimeter is 20 cm.
Compare 22, 18, 16 and 20. The smallest is 16 cm, so the least perimeter belongs to a rectangle with dimensions 5 cm and 3 cm.

misconceptions.A: The square's perimeter is 4 × 5.5 = 22 cm, which is the largest of the four. Work out the others and compare.
misconceptions.B: The triangle's perimeter is 3 × 6 = 18 cm, which is small, but one shape has less. Check the rectangle.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The rectangle's perimeter is 2 × (5 + 3) = 16 cm, the smallest of the four.
misconceptions.D: A rhombus has 4 equal sides, so its perimeter is 4 × 5 = 20 cm. One of the other shapes has less.

questionText: The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is equal to that of a square of side 6 cm. What is the side of the triangle?
hints: Two shapes have the same perimeter here. Find the perimeter of the shape you know everything about, then use it for the other shape.
A square has four equal sides. Work out the perimeter of the square with side 6 cm first.

Here is a similar one: an equilateral triangle has the same perimeter as a square of side 9 cm. The square's perimeter is 4 × 9 = 36 cm. The triangle has three equal sides, so each side is 36 ÷ 3 = 12 cm.

stepByStep.text: The square has four equal sides of 6 cm, so its perimeter is 4 × 6 = 24 cm.
The triangle has the same perimeter, 24 cm.
An equilateral triangle has three equal sides, so each side is 24 ÷ 3 = 8.
The side of the triangle is 8 cm.

misconceptions.A: 18 comes from 3 × 6, giving the triangle sides of 6 cm. The perimeters are equal, not the sides, so find the square's perimeter first.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The square's perimeter is 4 × 6 = 24 cm, and 24 ÷ 3 = 8 cm for each side of the triangle.
misconceptions.C: 4 comes from 24 ÷ 6, dividing the perimeter by the square's side. Share the perimeter among the triangle's three equal sides.
misconceptions.D: 2 comes from 6 ÷ 3, sharing one side of the square. Find the whole perimeter of the square before you share it.

questionText: Each side of a square is 19 cm long. What is the area of the square?
hints: This asks for the area of a square, the space inside it. All the sides of a square are equal.
For a square, area is side × side. Set up 19 × 19.
Here is a similar one: a square with side 7 cm. Area = 7 × 7 = 49 cm².

stepByStep.text: The area of a square is side × side.
Split 19 into 10 and 9. Multiply 19 by 10.
Now multiply 19 by 9.
Add the two parts. So the area is 361 cm².

misconceptions.A: This is 19 × 3. For area, multiply the side by itself: 19 × 19.
misconceptions.B: This is 19 too many, like one extra row. Work out 19 × 19 once more.
misconceptions.C: This is double the area. Multiply the side by itself just once.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 19 × 19 = 361, so the area is 361 cm².

questionText: The area of a square is equal to the area of a rectangle whose length and breadth are 16 cm and 4 cm. Find the perimeter of the square.
hints: There are three stages here: the area of the rectangle, then the side of the square with the same area, then the perimeter of that square.
Multiply 16 by 4 to get the rectangle's area. Then look for a number that, multiplied by itself, gives that area.
Similar example: a square has the same area as a rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm. The area is 9 × 4 = 36 square cm. Since 6 × 6 = 36, the square's side is 6 cm, and its perimeter is 4 × 6 = 24 cm.

stepByStep.text: Find the area of the rectangle.
The square has the same area, 64 square cm. Since 8 × 8 = 64, the side of the square is 8 cm.
The perimeter of a square is 4 times its side.
The perimeter of the square is 32 cm.

misconceptions.A: 16 cm is the rectangle's length. Find the rectangle's area, then the square's side, then 4 times that side.
misconceptions.B: 8 cm is the side of the square. The question asks for the perimeter, so multiply by 4.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The area is 64 square cm, the side is 8 cm, and 4 × 8 = 32.
misconceptions.D: 64 is the area in square cm. Find the side that multiplied by itself gives 64, then go round the four sides.

questionText: The perimeter of a square equals the perimeter of a rectangle with length 16 cm and breadth 4 cm. Find the area of the square.
hints: There are three stages here: the perimeter of the rectangle, then the side of the square with the same perimeter, then the area of that square.
Find the rectangle's perimeter by adding 16 and 4 and doubling. Then share that perimeter equally among the 4 sides of the square.

Similar example: a square has the same perimeter as a rectangle 9 cm by 3 cm. The rectangle's perimeter is 2 × (9 + 3) = 24 cm. The square's side is 24 ÷ 4 = 6 cm, so its area is 6 × 6 = 36 square cm.

stepByStep.text: Find the perimeter of the rectangle.
The square has the same perimeter. Share 40 cm among its 4 equal sides.
The area of a square is side times side.
The area of the square is 100 sq. cm.

misconceptions.A: 256 is 16 × 16, which uses the rectangle's length as the square's side. The square's side comes from sharing the perimeter among 4 sides.
misconceptions.B: 400 is 20 × 20. 20 is the length plus the breadth, but the full perimeter is 40 cm, and each side of the square is a quarter of that.
misconceptions.C: 10 cm is the side of the square. For the area, multiply the side by itself.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The perimeter is 40 cm, the side is 10 cm, and 10 × 10 = 100.

questionText: A rectangle is 12 cm long and 11 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the rectangle. Remember that a rectangle has two lengths and two widths.
Add the length and the width first: 12 + 11. Then think about how many of each side there are.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 15 cm long and 10 cm wide. 15 + 10 = 25. Double it: 25 × 2 = 50 cm.

stepByStep.text: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. Start by adding the length and the width.
There are two lengths and two widths, so double it. The perimeter is 46 cm.

misconceptions.A: This is close, but 3 too many. Add 12 and 11 again, then double the total.
misconceptions.B: This counts the length three times. Use two lengths and two widths only.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 12 + 11 = 23, and double that is 46 cm.
misconceptions.D: This is 12 + 11, just one length and one width. There are two of each, so double it.

questionText: A rectangle is 25 cm long and 16 cm wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length × width. Set up 25 × 16 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 11 cm long and 7 cm wide. Area = 11 × 7 = 77 cm².

stepByStep.text: The area of a rectangle is length × width.
Split 16 into 10 and 6. Multiply 25 by 10.
Now multiply 25 by 6.
Add the two parts. So the area is 400 cm².

misconceptions.A: Yes! 25 × 16 = 400, so the area is 400 cm².
misconceptions.B: This is half of the area. Multiply the full length by the full width.
misconceptions.C: This is 25 + 16. For area you multiply the length by the width.
misconceptions.D: This is 25 too many, like one extra row. Work out 25 × 16 once more.

questionText: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are:
hints: Think about what a parallelogram looks like: a rectangle that has been pushed over to one side. Look at each pair of sides that face each other.
The name of the shape gives a clue about one property of its opposite sides. Then think about whether the two sides facing each other are the same length.

Similar example: in a trapezium, one pair of opposite sides is parallel, but those two sides are not the same length, and the other pair is not parallel at all. Ask the same two questions about a parallelogram: are the opposite sides parallel, and are they equal? Drawing one will help.

stepByStep.text: The word parallelogram comes from the word parallel. Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, which means they run in the same direction and never meet.
Measure the sides of any parallelogram and you find that each side is the same length as the side facing it.
So in a parallelogram, opposite sides are parallel and equal.

misconceptions.A: The equal part is right. Opposite sides of a parallelogram are also parallel, which is where its name comes from.
misconceptions.B: Yes! In a parallelogram each pair of opposite sides is both parallel and equal.
misconceptions.C: A parallelogram has both properties. Its opposite sides never meet, and they are the same length.
misconceptions.D: The parallel part is right. The opposite sides are also the same length, so check that part again.

questionText: In a rhombus, the axes of symmetry are:

options.text: there are no axes of symmetry

hints: An axis of symmetry is a fold line. When you fold the shape along it, the two halves lie exactly on top of each other.
Picture a rhombus, a shape like a diamond with four equal sides. Imagine folding it from one corner to the opposite corner. Do the two halves match?

Here is a similar one: what are the axes of symmetry of a rectangle? Folding it along a diagonal does not make the halves match. Folding it along the line joining the middles of two opposite sides does. So a rectangle's axes of symmetry are the two lines through the middles of opposite sides.

stepByStep.text: An axis of symmetry is a line along which a shape can be folded so that the two halves match exactly.
A rhombus has four equal sides. If you fold it along the line joining two opposite corners, the two halves match.
This works for both pairs of opposite corners, and those two lines are the diagonals.
So the axes of symmetry of a rhombus are the diagonals.

misconceptions.A: A rhombus does have fold lines that make its halves match. Try folding it from one corner to the opposite corner.
misconceptions.B: An angle is a corner, not a line, so it cannot be a fold line. Look for lines that pass through the corners.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Folding a rhombus along either diagonal makes the two halves match exactly.
misconceptions.D: A side is an edge of the rhombus, so you cannot fold the shape in half along it. An axis of symmetry passes through the middle of the shape.

questionText: Which of the following statements is TRUE?
hints: Each statement says that every shape of one kind is also a shape of another kind. To test one, ask whether the first shape always has everything the second shape needs.

Write down what each shape needs. A rectangle needs four right angles. A square needs four right angles and four equal sides. A rhombus needs four equal sides. A parallelogram needs two pairs of parallel sides.

Similar example: is every square a rhombus? A rhombus needs four equal sides. Every square has four equal sides, so every square is a rhombus. Test each statement in the same way, by checking what the second shape needs.

stepByStep.text: A rectangle is a four-sided shape with four right angles. A square has four right angles and also four equal sides.
Every square has four right angles, so every square has all that a rectangle needs.

The other statements can each be shown untrue with one drawing: a slanted rhombus has no right angles, a slanted parallelogram has no right angles, and a long rectangle does not have four equal sides.
The true statement is: Every square is a rectangle.

misconceptions.A: A rhombus has four equal sides but can be slanted, with no right angles. A square needs right angles too.
misconceptions.B: Yes! A square has four right angles, which is all a rectangle needs.
misconceptions.C: A parallelogram can lean over, so its angles need not be right angles. A rectangle needs four right angles.
misconceptions.D: A rectangle can be longer than it is broad. A square needs all four sides equal.

questionText: A rectangle is 26 cm long and 24 cm wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length × width. Set up 26 × 24 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 12 cm long and 5 cm wide. Area = 12 × 5 = 60 cm².

stepByStep.text: The area of a rectangle is length × width.
Split 24 into 20 and 4. Multiply 26 by 20.
Now multiply 26 by 4.
Add the two parts. So the area is 624 cm².

misconceptions.A: Yes! 26 × 24 = 624, so the area is 624 cm².

questionText: A kite has how many axes of symmetry?

Fold along the other corner-to-corner line. A short side would land on a long side, so the halves do not match.
A kite has 1 axis of symmetry.

questionText: The diagonals of a square:

hints: A diagonal joins opposite corners. Think about two things: whether the two diagonals of a square are the same length, and how they cross each other.
